subtopic_detail: Action on new neutropenia during weekly monitoring in an established clozapine patient with schizophrenia
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar at a community clozapine clinic. A 34 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia has been on clozapine 400 mg nocte for 3 years with good clinical response. His routine full blood count today (week 156 of therapy) shows a neutrophil count of 1.2 x10^9/L (previously 3.8 x10^9/L last week). White cell count is 3.0 x10^9/L. He has no fever, sore throat or infection.

He reports having had a viral upper respiratory infection with his 3 year old daughter 5 days ago and both have recovered. He denies missed doses and there has been no dose change. He has no other medication and does not smoke. He is asymptomatic and clinically well today. He lives 40 minutes from the hospital with his partner and has reliable transport.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Laboratory: Neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L (prior 3.8), white cell count 3.0, no left shift, haemoglobin 148 g/L, platelets 265
data_table.Clinical: Asymptomatic, no fever or infection, no missed doses, viral upper respiratory infection with child 5 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Continue clozapine and start prophylactic oral amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid 875 mg twice daily for 7 days to prevent bacterial infection due to the low neutrophil count reading
options.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated at amber alert without clinical infection; empirical antibiotics only if febrile neutropenia develops. (Source: TGA Clozapine Haematological Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately today, admit to hospital for reverse isolation and start intravenous filgrastim 300 mcg subcutaneously daily for suspected clozapine induced agranulocytosis
options.rationale: Cessation is required only at red alert (neutrophils below 1.0); amber alert level allows continuation with closer monitoring; filgrastim is not first line here. (Source: TGA Clozapine Haematological Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 200 mg nocte and switch to alternative agent olanzapine 20 mg orally daily immediately because dose reduction alone reverses clozapine haematological toxicity effectively
options.rationale: Dose reduction does not reliably reverse clozapine haematological effects; switching in a treatment resistant patient risks relapse and is not indicated at amber alert. (Source: TGA Clozapine Haematological Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Continue clozapine at current dose and defer any additional full blood count until his routine weekly test next week because a viral infection can transiently reduce neutrophil count
options.rationale: Amber alert (neutrophils 1.0 to 1.5) mandates increased monitoring frequency; deferring to routine weekly testing does not meet AU protocol. (Source: TGA Clozapine Haematological Monitoring Guidance)

options.text: Continue clozapine, increase monitoring to twice weekly full blood count and review neutrophil count within 48 hours as per the Australian amber alert protocol
options.rationale: Neutrophils 1.0 to 1.5 x10^9/L is an amber alert; clozapine can continue with twice weekly monitoring under close review per AU protocol. (Source: TGA Clozapine Haematological Monitoring Guidance)

explanation.summary: Clozapine requires haematological monitoring because of the risk of neutropenia and agranulocytosis, especially in the first 18 weeks. The TGA registry uses a three colour alert system based on neutrophil count. Green alert (neutrophils 2.0 x10^9/L or higher) is normal weekly then monthly monitoring after 18 weeks. Amber alert (1.5 to 1.99 x10^9/L or a rapid fall) requires twice weekly full blood count while continuing clozapine and clinical review. Red alert (neutrophils below 1.0 x10^9/L or white cell count below 2.0) requires immediate cessation, daily full blood count, infection screening, and consideration of filgrastim and non rechallenge. Intercurrent illness can transiently reduce counts.
key_points: AU registry alert system: green greater than 2.0, amber 1.5 to 1.99, red below 1.0 x10^9/L neutrophils.
Amber alert: continue clozapine with twice weekly full blood count monitoring.
Red alert: cease clozapine, daily monitoring and consider filgrastim; usually no rechallenge.
explanation.pearls: Amber alert on clozapine (neutrophils 1.0 to 1.99 x10^9/L): continue the drug and switch to twice weekly full blood count with clinical review; cease only at red alert below 1.0.

subtopic_detail: First line therapy for post traumatic stress disorder 6 months after a single traumatic event
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42 year old woman 6 months after a motor vehicle collision. She meets DSM 5 criteria for post traumatic stress disorder with re-experiencing (nightmares 4 times per week), avoidance of driving on major roads, hyperarousal and negative mood. She has not been able to return to work as a delivery driver. She has no active suicidal ideation. She does not use alcohol or illicit substances.

She has no personal or family psychiatric history and is on no medication. She has private health insurance and access to a trauma trained psychologist within 4 weeks. She has full mental capacity and is engaged in her own care planning. She has no other significant medical conditions or allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Assessment: DSM 5 PTSD, chronic, single event, no comorbid substance use, no active suicidal ideation, no psychosis
data_table.Access: Trauma trained psychologist available within 4 weeks, mental capacity intact, motivated for treatment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing weekly for 8 to 12 sessions with a trauma trained psychologist starting now
options.rationale: First line for chronic PTSD is trauma focused psychological therapy; pharmacotherapy is added if therapy is inaccessible, not responding, or comorbid depression. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guideline)

options.text: Sertraline 50 mg orally daily as first line monotherapy in preference to psychological therapy because pharmacotherapy achieves faster and more durable remission of core PTSD symptoms
options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not more effective than trauma focused therapy; psychological therapy is first line where accessible. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guideline)

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg orally as needed for anxiety and prazosin 1 mg nocte for nightmares in a chronic PTSD monotherapy regimen while awaiting the psychology appointment weeks away
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes and are not recommended; prazosin is an adjunct not monotherapy. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guideline)

options.text: Single session psychological debriefing at 6 months after the event to allow processing of the trauma memory before starting a course of formal weekly psychology
options.rationale: Single session debriefing is not recommended and can worsen symptoms; structured trauma focused therapy is the appropriate intervention. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guideline)

options.text: Mirtazapine 30 mg nocte primarily for improved sleep alone, with an anticipated indirect improvement in the daytime PTSD symptoms over the next 8 weeks of monotherapy
options.rationale: Mirtazapine may help sleep and depression but is not first line for core PTSD symptoms; trauma focused therapy is preferred. (Source: Phoenix Australia PTSD Guideline)

explanation.summary: The Australian Phoenix guideline recommends trauma focused psychological therapy (trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing) as first line for adults with post traumatic stress disorder when accessible. Typical course is 8 to 12 weekly sessions with a trained clinician. Pharmacotherapy (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as sertraline or paroxetine, or venlafaxine) is considered when psychological therapy is unavailable, declined or ineffective, or when a comorbid disorder such as depression justifies it. Adjuncts include prazosin for nightmares. Benzodiazepines are avoided because they worsen outcomes. Single session debriefing is not recommended.
key_points: First line: trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are second line or when therapy inaccessible.
Benzodiazepines worsen outcomes and are avoided; single session debriefing is not recommended.
explanation.pearls: Chronic PTSD 6 months post trauma with access to a trained psychologist: refer for 8 to 12 weeks of trauma focused cognitive behavioural therapy or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing as first line.

subtopic_detail: Refeeding management of a severely underweight adolescent with anorexia nervosa admitted for medical stabilisation
stem:
You are the paediatric medical registrar admitting a 15 year old girl with anorexia nervosa. She is 158 cm tall and weighs 34 kg (body mass index 13.6, less than 70 percent of expected body weight for age and height). She has been eating less than 500 kcal per day for 3 weeks and has lost 6 kg in 2 months. She has amenorrhoea for 4 months.

On admission she has bradycardia (pulse 42 /min), hypothermia and postural drop from 108/68 to 88/56 mmHg. She is alert and cooperative. Bedside electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a corrected QT of 460 ms. Bloods show phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.5), magnesium 0.7 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.1), potassium 3.4 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42 /min, blood pressure 108/68 lying and 88/56 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 35.6 degC
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus bradycardia, corrected QT interval 460 ms, no ventricular ectopy on cardiac monitoring
data_table.Laboratory: Phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (0.75 to 1.5), magnesium 0.7 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.1), potassium 3.4 mmol/L, glucose 3.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding plan?

options.text: Start high calorie feeding at 3000 kcal/day immediately to reverse malnutrition faster and check phosphate weekly for four weeks throughout the inpatient rehabilitation stay
options.rationale: Very high initial calories risk refeeding hypophosphataemia and cardiac arrhythmia; monitoring must be daily initially, not weekly. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Start oral thiamine 100 mg daily, correct electrolytes prophylactically and begin 1400 kcal/day of balanced diet with daily electrolyte monitoring on cardiac telemetry
options.rationale: AU eating disorder guidance for severely malnourished adolescents is start at 1000 to 1500 kcal/day with thiamine, prophylactic electrolyte correction and daily monitoring on telemetry to prevent refeeding syndrome. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Withhold all oral feeding for 48 hours to normalise glucose and electrolytes and start intravenous 5 percent dextrose infusion in the meantime for adequate nutrition support
options.rationale: Delaying feeding worsens the medical state; intravenous dextrose alone without thiamine and electrolyte cover precipitates refeeding syndrome. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube for continuous overnight parenteral nutrition at 40 mL/hour and defer any daytime oral intake to standardise the caloric intake exactly overnight
options.rationale: Nasogastric refeeding is not parenteral nutrition; and oral intake should be encouraged; the described plan does not follow AU practice. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Discharge with weekly outpatient dietitian review because she is medically stable given normal sodium, glucose and phosphate results at admission before any weight gain has occurred
options.rationale: Body mass index 13.6, bradycardia, postural drop and corrected QT 460 ms meet AU criteria for medical admission; discharge is unsafe. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, cardiac arrhythmia, Wernicke encephalopathy) is the major early risk when starting nutrition in severely malnourished patients. Australian guidance for adolescents with anorexia nervosa and body mass index below 14, rapid weight loss, or medical instability (bradycardia below 50, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, prolonged corrected QT) is inpatient medical stabilisation. Start feeding at 1000 to 1500 kcal/day (or higher under strict monitoring in some protocols), give oral thiamine 100 mg daily, prophylactically correct phosphate, magnesium and potassium, monitor electrolytes daily for the first week, and use continuous cardiac telemetry. Weight gain target is 0.5 to 1 kg per week.
key_points: Refeeding risks: hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, cardiac arrhythmia, Wernicke encephalopathy.
Start 1000 to 1500 kcal/day, thiamine 100 mg daily, prophylactic electrolyte correction.
Daily electrolytes, cardiac telemetry, target 0.5 to 1 kg weight gain per week.
explanation.pearls: Anorexia nervosa admission at body mass index 13.6 with bradycardia and prolonged corrected QT: start 1400 kcal/day, thiamine 100 mg, prophylactic electrolyte correction and daily monitoring on cardiac telemetry.

subtopic_detail: Rule out chest pain pathway in a low risk patient with a normal initial high sensitivity troponin
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 54 year old man presents with 90 minutes of central chest heaviness that came on at rest and has now resolved after arrival. He has hypertension controlled on amlodipine and is an ex smoker of 10 pack years, stopped 5 years ago. He has no diabetes. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 68.

On examination he is comfortable and pain free. Cardiac and respiratory examination is unremarkable. Electrocardiogram at triage 30 minutes after pain onset shows sinus rhythm with no ST or T wave abnormalities. High sensitivity troponin I taken on arrival (2 hours after pain onset) is 6 ng/L (99th centile 26 ng/L for men).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm, no ST or T wave abnormalities, no bundle branch block, no Q waves
data_table.Troponin: High sensitivity troponin I 6 ng/L at 2 hours post pain onset (99th centile 26 ng/L for men)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home now without further troponin testing because a single normal high sensitivity troponin I at 2 hours after pain onset excludes myocardial infarction reliably in low risk patients
options.rationale: A single troponin is not sufficient to rule out infarction; the algorithm requires repeat testing at 1 hour or 3 hours per Australian pathway. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Admit to coronary care unit for 24 hours of continuous cardiac telemetry monitoring and repeat high sensitivity troponin I every 6 hours for two more measurements before decision
options.rationale: The 0 and 1 hour algorithm has replaced the 0, 6 and 12 hour pathway for low risk chest pain in AU; admission to coronary care unit is not needed if algorithm rules out infarction. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Repeat high sensitivity troponin I at 1 hour with electrocardiogram, and if unchanged and asymptomatic discharge on outpatient exercise stress test within 72 hours
options.rationale: For low risk chest pain the 0 and 1 hour high sensitivity troponin algorithm can rule out acute myocardial infarction and allow discharge with early outpatient functional testing. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Start aspirin 300 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose and refer for urgent coronary angiography within the next 24 hours in this patient with an intermediate risk assessment
options.rationale: There is no ischaemic evidence on electrocardiogram or troponin; dual antiplatelet loading and angiography are premature. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Arrange outpatient coronary computed tomography angiography within 7 days without further troponin testing because normal appearance excludes obstructive coronary artery disease reliably now
options.rationale: Coronary computed tomography angiography is an option after safe rule out but does not replace the acute troponin algorithm; the acute pathway must be completed first. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

explanation.summary: Contemporary Australian chest pain pathways use the 0 and 1 hour (or 0 and 2 hour) high sensitivity troponin algorithm to rapidly rule out or rule in acute myocardial infarction in low risk patients. Rule out requires a very low initial troponin with unchanged repeat and no dynamic electrocardiogram change; patients can then be discharged on early outpatient functional testing (exercise stress test or coronary computed tomography angiography) within 72 hours. Rule in is a rising troponin above the 99th centile in a compatible clinical setting. Intermediate results (indeterminate zone) require serial testing at 3 hours and admission. The 0, 6, 12 hour pathway is no longer standard.
key_points: Rule out uses 0 and 1 (or 0 and 2) hour high sensitivity troponin algorithm plus electrocardiogram.
Rule out patients get outpatient functional testing within 72 hours.
Rule in is a rising troponin above the 99th centile with compatible clinical picture.
explanation.pearls: Low risk chest pain resolved with normal initial high sensitivity troponin and no electrocardiogram change: repeat troponin at 1 hour and discharge for early outpatient stress test within 72 hours if unchanged.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Acute Coronary Syndromes

subtopic_detail: Addition of a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor to established guideline therapy in symptomatic HFrEF without diabetes
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in a heart failure outpatient clinic. A 68 year old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (ischaemic aetiology, ejection fraction 32 percent) is on maximally tolerated sacubitril valsartan 97/103 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 10 mg daily and spironolactone 25 mg daily. He remains New York Heart Association class II with breathlessness on climbing one flight of stairs. His weight is stable.

He has no diabetes. His most recent creatinine is 108 micromol/L (estimated glomerular filtration rate 62 mL/min/1.73 m2), potassium 4.5 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, and his blood pressure today is 118/72 mmHg. He has no history of urinary tract infection or diabetic ketoacidosis and no ketoacidosis risk factors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Cardiac: Sinus rhythm, S3 audible, no peripheral oedema, jugular venous pressure 3 cm above sternal angle
data_table.Renal: Creatinine 108 micromol/L (estimated glomerular filtration rate 62), potassium 4.5 mmol/L, no proteinuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Add ivabradine 5 mg orally twice daily because his New York Heart Association class II symptoms will improve with heart rate lowering below 70 /min beats regardless of current rate
options.rationale: Ivabradine is indicated only in sinus rhythm with heart rate 70 or higher on maximally tolerated beta blocker; his heart rate is 68 so ivabradine is not indicated. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

options.text: Add digoxin 125 mcg orally daily to reduce symptoms and heart failure hospitalisation as fourth line therapy after triple therapy is optimised in a patient without atrial fibrillation
options.rationale: Digoxin reduces hospitalisation but not mortality and is a later addition; sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are preferred as fourth line in HFrEF. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

options.text: Add oral furosemide 40 mg orally daily to address his ongoing New York Heart Association II symptoms of breathlessness on stairs and improve exercise tolerance without further changes now
options.rationale: Loop diuretics are for volume overload; he has no signs of congestion so a diuretic will not help and may worsen renal function. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

options.text: Add dapagliflozin 10 mg orally daily and continue current triple therapy, review for volume status and repeat renal function in 2 weeks after starting the new agent
options.rationale: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are recommended for HFrEF regardless of diabetes status once foundation triple therapy is optimised, reducing hospitalisation and mortality. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

options.text: Switch bisoprolol to metoprolol succinate 190 mg orally daily as it is a longer acting and more selective beta1 blocker for further improvement of the guideline directed medical therapy
options.rationale: Bisoprolol and metoprolol succinate are both first line beta blockers in AU; there is no benefit to switching between them at maximally tolerated dose. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Heart Failure Guideline)

explanation.summary: The Australian foundational quadruple therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is an angiotensin receptor neprilysin inhibitor or angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor, a beta blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol or metoprolol succinate), a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin). Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors reduce hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFrEF regardless of diabetes status, and are added once foundational triple therapy is optimised (or earlier in newly diagnosed patients). Ivabradine is added only in sinus rhythm with heart rate 70 or higher on maximally tolerated beta blocker. Digoxin is a later add on option.
key_points: AU foundational quadruple therapy: renin angiotensin blockade plus beta blocker plus mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist plus sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor benefit is independent of diabetes status.
Ivabradine requires sinus rhythm and heart rate 70 or higher on maximally tolerated beta blocker.
explanation.pearls: HFrEF on optimal triple therapy without a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor: add dapagliflozin 10 mg daily regardless of diabetes status and monitor volume and renal function in 2 weeks.

subtopic_detail: Timing of N acetylcysteine administration after acute single ingestion paracetamol overdose
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 22 year old woman is brought in by her flatmate 5 hours after ingesting 30 x 500 mg paracetamol tablets impulsively after an argument. She reports mild nausea and no vomiting. She weighs 60 kg and takes no regular medication. She has no history of chronic alcohol use, malnutrition or hepatic disease.

She is now alert and cooperative. Her mental state is settled and she is engaged with mental health assessment planning. Serum paracetamol at 4 hours post ingestion (drawn 45 minutes ago) is 195 mg/L, on or above the nomogram treatment line for a single acute ingestion. Alanine aminotransferase is 22 U/L (below 35), international normalised ratio 1.0, creatinine 68 micromol/L, venous pH 7.40.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 120/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Ingestion: 30 x 500 mg paracetamol 5 hours ago, single acute ingestion, no co-ingestion, weight 60 kg
data_table.Laboratory: Paracetamol 195 mg/L at 4 hours (on or above nomogram line), alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L, international normalised ratio 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Start intravenous N acetylcysteine using the 21 hour regimen without delay for the second bag while waiting for the exact bag calculations to be finalised on the ward
options.rationale: Paracetamol level above the nomogram treatment line requires immediate intravenous N acetylcysteine using the 21 hour regimen (150 mg/kg loading over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours). (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

options.text: Give oral activated charcoal 50 g now and repeat serum paracetamol at 8 hours before deciding on N acetylcysteine because charcoal is effective up to 8 hours post ingestion
options.rationale: Charcoal has limited benefit beyond 2 hours post ingestion; N acetylcysteine must not be delayed once the level is above the treatment line. (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

options.text: Give oral methionine 2.5 g every 4 hours for four doses in preference to intravenous N acetylcysteine because oral methionine has an equivalent hepatoprotective effect with fewer side effects
options.rationale: Oral methionine is not first line in AU; intravenous N acetylcysteine is standard and more reliable. (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

options.text: Give a single 5 g bolus of intravenous N acetylcysteine and then repeat serum paracetamol at 20 hours to determine whether further doses of N acetylcysteine are required
options.rationale: A single bolus is not sufficient; the AU regimen is a 3 bag protocol over 21 hours as a minimum. (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

options.text: Observe for 24 hours with 6 hourly liver function testing and only start N acetylcysteine if alanine aminotransferase rises above 100 U/L to reduce anaphylactoid reaction risk today
options.rationale: Waiting for liver enzymes to rise delays a hepatoprotective effect; the nomogram treatment line is the trigger, not enzyme rise. (Source: eTG Complete: Paracetamol Poisoning)

explanation.summary: Acute single ingestion of paracetamol is assessed with a serum paracetamol level drawn at 4 hours post ingestion or on presentation if later, and plotted on the Rumack Matthew nomogram (AU treatment line 150 mg/L at 4 hours). Levels on or above the line require immediate intravenous N acetylcysteine using the 21 hour regimen: 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours. High risk ingestion, staggered ingestion, or presentation over 8 hours after ingestion trigger empirical N acetylcysteine while awaiting the level. Ongoing hepatotoxicity or persistent elevation of alanine aminotransferase or international normalised ratio prompts continuation beyond 21 hours.
key_points: Treatment line: 150 mg/L at 4 hours (nomogram); N acetylcysteine indicated if on or above.
21 hour regimen: 150 mg/kg over 1 hour, then 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours.
Empirical N acetylcysteine if presentation over 8 hours, staggered ingestion or high risk regardless of level.
explanation.pearls: Paracetamol level above the treatment line: start the 21 hour intravenous N acetylcysteine regimen without delay (150 then 50 then 100 mg/kg) and monitor liver enzymes and international normalised ratio.

subtopic_detail: Choice of pharmacological venous thromboembolism prophylaxis on admission with community acquired pneumonia
stem:
You are the general medicine intern admitting a 76 year old woman with severe community acquired pneumonia. She is on 2 L/min nasal oxygen for SpO2 92 percent and needs intravenous ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. Her mobility is limited and she is expected to stay 5 to 7 days. Her body mass index is 28. She has never had venous thromboembolism.

Her bloods show creatinine 88 micromol/L (estimated glomerular filtration rate 58 mL/min/1.73 m2), platelets 220 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L (115 to 165), international normalised ratio 1.0. She is on aspirin 100 mg daily for previous transient ischaemic attack. She has no active bleeding, no epidural, no scheduled surgery, and no allergy to heparin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 92% on 2 L nasal oxygen, temperature 38.4 degC
data_table.Mobility: Limited, expected stay 5 to 7 days, no active bleeding, no epidural, no scheduled surgery
data_table.Laboratory: Estimated glomerular filtration rate 58 mL/min/1.73 m2, platelets 220 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L, international normalised ratio 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate venous thromboembolism prophylaxis?

options.text: Continue her aspirin 100 mg daily as her only pharmacological prophylaxis because it also gives some protection against venous thromboembolism at the same medication level as before
options.rationale: Aspirin is not adequate venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for acute medical illness with reduced mobility; low molecular weight heparin is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

options.text: Subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily starting on admission and continuing while her mobility is reduced, alongside mechanical prophylaxis with graduated compression stockings
options.rationale: Acute medical illness with reduced mobility warrants low molecular weight heparin as first line venous thromboembolism prophylaxis with mechanical prophylaxis as an adjunct. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

options.text: Give apixaban 2.5 mg orally twice daily throughout the admission because direct oral anticoagulants provide reliable prophylaxis in acute medical illness of any inpatient
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are not TGA approved for acute medical inpatient venous thromboembolism prophylaxis; low molecular weight heparin remains first line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

options.text: Mechanical prophylaxis with graduated compression stockings alone and repeat risk assessment daily because pharmacological prophylaxis is not needed unless bed rest exceeds seven days
options.rationale: Mechanical prophylaxis alone is used when pharmacological therapy is contraindicated (active bleeding, thrombocytopenia below 50); this patient has no contraindication to heparin. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

options.text: Subcutaneous unfractionated heparin 5000 units three times daily in preference to enoxaparin because unfractionated heparin has a shorter half life and is preferred in the elderly
options.rationale: Unfractionated heparin is used when renal function is severely impaired or if surgery is imminent; low molecular weight heparin is preferred at estimated glomerular filtration rate over 30. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: VTE Prophylaxis)

explanation.summary: Hospitalised medical patients with reduced mobility and one or more additional venous thromboembolism risk factors (age over 60, cancer, prior venous thromboembolism, obesity, thrombophilia, acute infection or heart failure) require pharmacological prophylaxis unless contraindicated. In Australia the first line is subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg once daily (or dalteparin 5000 units daily); unfractionated heparin 5000 units subcutaneous every 8 hours is reserved for severe renal impairment (estimated glomerular filtration rate under 30) or when frequent invasive procedures are anticipated. Mechanical prophylaxis (graduated compression stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression) is used as an adjunct or as monotherapy when pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated. Direct oral anticoagulants are not routinely used for medical inpatient prophylaxis in AU.
key_points: First line: enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous daily plus mechanical prophylaxis when indicated.
Unfractionated heparin for severe renal impairment or imminent invasive procedures.
Mechanical prophylaxis alone if pharmacological is contraindicated (active bleeding, thrombocytopenia).
explanation.pearls: Acute medical admission with reduced mobility and no contraindication: start subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily and add mechanical prophylaxis; use unfractionated heparin only if the estimated glomerular filtration rate is below 30.

sources.label: ANZ Working Party Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism

subtopic_detail: Immediate management sequence for hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes in a chronic kidney disease patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar. A 74 year old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate 22 mL/min/1.73 m2) presents feeling weak and lightheaded. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin and ramipril, and he takes spironolactone for heart failure. Last week his general practitioner started trimethoprim 300 mg daily for a urinary tract infection.

His venous potassium today is 7.2 mmol/L (verified on repeat sample), sodium 138 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, urea 24 mmol/L, creatinine 320 micromol/L. Electrocardiogram shows peaked T waves in V2 to V4 with mildly prolonged PR interval, no widened QRS and no arrhythmia. He is alert but weak. He weighs 78 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 62 /min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Peaked T waves V2 to V4, PR interval mildly prolonged, no widened QRS, no arrhythmia
data_table.Laboratory: Potassium 7.2 mmol/L (repeat verified), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, urea 24 mmol/L, creatinine 320 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management sequence?

options.text: Give oral polystyrene sulfonate 15 g four times daily and repeat serum potassium in 4 hours because oral resin lowers potassium reliably and avoids the intravenous access requirement
options.rationale: Oral polystyrene sulfonate has slow onset and does not treat acute hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes; intravenous therapy is needed first. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg over 10 minutes as first line therapy because inhaled beta 2 agonists shift potassium intracellularly rapidly and are safer than intravenous calcium at his age
options.rationale: Salbutamol is an adjunct, not first line when there are electrocardiogram changes; calcium is given first to protect the myocardium. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 minutes, then intravenous actrapid 10 units in 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose over 15 minutes, cease ramipril, spironolactone and trimethoprim
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes needs calcium first for cardiac membrane stabilisation, then insulin dextrose to shift potassium, plus removal of offending drugs. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Intravenous 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate 100 mL over 30 minutes as first line therapy in a normal blood pressure patient because it shifts potassium intracellularly more reliably than insulin
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate has limited effect on potassium unless there is severe metabolic acidosis; it is not first line and does not replace calcium and insulin. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis without any medical therapy because chronic kidney disease with potassium 7.2 mmol/L and electrocardiogram changes needs dialysis and calcium and insulin delay definitive treatment
options.rationale: Dialysis is definitive but takes time to organise; calcium and insulin dextrose must not be delayed while dialysis is arranged. (Source: eTG Complete: Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Acute hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes (peaked T waves, PR prolongation, widened QRS, sinus wave morphology) requires stepwise emergency management. First, cardiac membrane stabilisation with intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 minutes (or calcium chloride 10 percent 10 mL via central access), repeated at 5 minutes if changes persist. Second, potassium shift into cells with intravenous actrapid 10 units in 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose over 15 minutes, plus nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg. Third, potassium removal with intravenous furosemide (if volume permits), potassium binders (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or patiromer), or dialysis in severe or refractory hyperkalaemia. Fourth, remove precipitants (angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists, non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, trimethoprim, potassium supplements).
key_points: First: intravenous calcium for cardiac membrane stabilisation when electrocardiogram is abnormal.
Second: intravenous insulin dextrose (and nebulised salbutamol) to shift potassium.
Third: remove potassium by diuretic, binders or dialysis; stop precipitants.
explanation.pearls: Potassium 7.2 mmol/L with peaked T waves on chronic kidney disease and drug precipitants: give intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL first, then insulin dextrose, and stop ramipril, spironolactone and trimethoprim now.

subtopic_detail: Selection of intravenous fluid transition in adult diabetic ketoacidosis with falling blood glucose
stem:
You are the medical registrar managing a 38 year old man with type 1 diabetes admitted 4 hours ago with diabetic ketoacidosis after intercurrent gastroenteritis. Initial pH was 7.14, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, blood glucose 26 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L and potassium 4.8 mmol/L. He has received 2 L of 0.9 percent saline (first over 1 hour, second over 2 hours), and a fixed rate intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour on 80 kg body weight (8 units/hour).

His latest labs at hour 4 show blood glucose 12 mmol/L, ketones 3.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L. He is alert and volume replete with normal blood pressure. He is on continuous cardiac monitoring. His current fluid is 0.9 percent saline at 250 mL/hour.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Biochemistry: Blood glucose 12 mmol/L, ketones 3.2 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L
data_table.Fluid balance: 2 L 0.9 percent saline received, current 0.9 percent saline at 250 mL/hour, insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour (8 units/hour)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his fluid and insulin regimen now?

options.text: Stop the intravenous insulin infusion, start subcutaneous long acting insulin glargine 20 units and short acting insulin aspart 6 units with meal to transition to subcutaneous care now
options.rationale: Transition to subcutaneous insulin requires ketones below 0.6, bicarbonate above 18 and the patient eating; he does not meet these criteria yet. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

options.text: Reduce the fixed rate insulin infusion from 0.1 to 0.03 units/kg/hour, continue 0.9 percent saline alone at 250 mL/hour and recheck ketones and blood glucose in one hour today
options.rationale: Reducing insulin will slow ketone clearance and prolong DKA; dextrose is added rather than insulin reduced. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

options.text: Change intravenous fluid from 0.9 percent saline to Hartmann solution to reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis and continue insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour without adding any dextrose to the regimen
options.rationale: Balanced crystalloid can be used to reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis but does not address the falling blood glucose; dextrose is still needed to allow ongoing insulin. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

options.text: Add 10 percent dextrose intravenous infusion at 125 mL/hour running alongside the saline, continue fixed rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour, and continue potassium replacement per protocol
options.rationale: When blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L in DKA, dextrose is added alongside the ongoing saline to allow the fixed rate insulin infusion to continue clearing ketones. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes to accelerate resolution of the metabolic acidosis and continue current fluid and insulin regimen unchanged for another hour
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is used only for pH under 7.0 or severe hyperkalaemia with instability; it does not accelerate DKA resolution. (Source: eTG Complete: DKA)

explanation.summary: In adult diabetic ketoacidosis management, the first priority is intravenous fluid resuscitation (usually 0.9 percent saline, though balanced crystalloid is acceptable), followed by fixed rate intravenous insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour, potassium replacement in the fluid when potassium is below 5.5 mmol/L, and hourly ketone and blood glucose monitoring. When blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L before ketones and bicarbonate have normalised, 10 percent dextrose is added at 125 mL/hour alongside the ongoing saline to allow insulin to continue clearing ketones. Transition to subcutaneous insulin is safe once ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate is above 18 mmol/L, pH is above 7.3, and the patient is eating. Long acting insulin is given before stopping the infusion to prevent rebound.
key_points: Add 10 percent dextrose at 125 mL/hour when blood glucose is below 14 mmol/L in DKA.
Do not reduce insulin infusion prematurely; keep at 0.1 units/kg/hour until ketones cleared.
Transition to subcutaneous insulin when ketones below 0.6, bicarbonate above 18 and eating.
explanation.pearls: DKA blood glucose falling below 14 mmol/L with ongoing ketosis: add 10 percent dextrose at 125 mL/hour alongside the saline and keep insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour until ketones clear.

subtopic_detail: Choice of vasopressor and access in septic shock with fluid unresponsive hypotension in emergency
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 68 year old man is brought in with 2 days of cough, fever and rigors. His blood pressure on arrival was 78/48 mmHg. He has received 30 mL/kg (2.5 L) of Hartmann solution over the last 90 minutes and blood cultures were drawn before intravenous piperacillin tazobactam 4.5 g. His initial venous lactate was 4.6 mmol/L. He weighs 80 kg.

After fluid resuscitation his blood pressure remains 82/50 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg), pulse 118 /min, respiratory rate 28 /min, SpO2 93 percent on 6 L/min facemask, temperature 38.9 degC. Repeat venous lactate is 3.8 mmol/L. He is orientated but drowsy (Glasgow Coma Score 14). A peripheral 18 gauge cannula is patent in his right cubital fossa. Chest x-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 60), respiratory rate 28, SpO2 93% on 6 L/min facemask, temperature 38.9 degC
data_table.Access: Peripheral 18 gauge cannula in right cubital fossa, no central line, no arterial line yet
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 3.8 mmol/L (from 4.6), right lower lobe consolidation on chest x-ray, urine output 15 mL over the past hour

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a stat dose of intravenous adrenaline 1 mg immediately for the shock and delay noradrenaline for after intubation because he is drowsy and needs airway protection first now
options.rationale: Bolus adrenaline 1 mg is for cardiac arrest, not septic shock; airway protection can proceed alongside vasopressor initiation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Give a further 2 L Hartmann over the next hour before starting any vasopressor because the lactate is still elevated and additional fluid resuscitation may improve mean arterial pressure adequately
options.rationale: Further large volume fluid after 30 mL/kg risks pulmonary oedema; noradrenaline is added to achieve mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Start dopamine infusion at 5 mcg/kg/min via the peripheral cannula because it improves renal perfusion and blood pressure in septic shock with acute kidney injury and low urine output
options.rationale: Dopamine is no longer first line for septic shock due to increased arrhythmia risk without mortality benefit; noradrenaline is preferred. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg over 24 hours as first line before starting any vasopressor because corticosteroid alone may reverse the vasoplegia of septic shock rapidly
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added when hypotension persists despite noradrenaline at 0.25 mcg/kg/min or higher; it is not used before vasopressor initiation. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Start noradrenaline infusion via peripheral cannula while arranging urgent central venous access, aiming mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg, and call intensive care now
options.rationale: Septic shock unresponsive to 30 mL/kg fluids needs noradrenaline first line; peripheral use is safe temporarily while central access is arranged. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Septic shock is defined as sepsis requiring vasopressor to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg or higher with a lactate above 2 mmol/L after adequate fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg crystalloid in the first hour). First line vasopressor is noradrenaline, titrated to a mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg. Peripheral administration is acceptable temporarily via a well sited proximal cannula while central venous access is arranged, and an arterial line is placed for accurate monitoring. Second line agents are vasopressin 0.03 units/min (or adrenaline) added when noradrenaline exceeds around 0.25 mcg/kg/min. Hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours is added when hypotension persists on noradrenaline at 0.25 mcg/kg/min or higher.
key_points: Septic shock: vasopressor plus lactate above 2 mmol/L after 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation.
First line vasopressor is noradrenaline targeting a mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg.
Peripheral noradrenaline is safe temporarily while central access and arterial line are arranged.
explanation.pearls: Septic shock unresponsive to 30 mL/kg Hartmann with mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg: start peripheral noradrenaline immediately, target mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg and call intensive care.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Sepsis in Adults
